questions.question: Why are B-trees preferred over binary search trees for database indexes?
options: B-trees are simpler to implement
B-trees have a high branching factor, reducing tree height and minimizing disk reads
Binary search trees cannot store strings
B-trees use less memory than binary search trees
questions.explanation: A binary search tree with N keys has height O(log2 N), requiring many disk reads. A B-tree node holds hundreds of keys, giving a branching factor of hundreds. This means millions of keys fit in just 3-4 levels, requiring only 3-4 disk reads per lookup.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of a lookup in a B-tree with N keys?
options: O(log N)
O(N)
O(N log N)
questions.explanation: A B-tree lookup traverses from root to leaf, visiting O(log N) nodes. At each node, a binary search among the keys takes O(log B) where B is the branching factor. Since B is constant, the overall complexity is O(log N).

questions.question: In an LSM tree, where do writes go first?
options: Directly to an SSTable on disk
To an in-memory sorted structure called a memtable
To a B-tree index
To a write-ahead log only
questions.explanation: LSM trees buffer writes in an in-memory memtable (typically a red-black tree or skip list). This makes writes extremely fast since they avoid disk I/O. When the memtable fills up, it's flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable.

questions.question: What is an SSTable and why is it sorted?
options: A SQL Server Table that stores schema metadata
A Sorted String Table — sorted order enables efficient merging and binary search lookups on disk
A Secure Socket Table used for encrypted connections
A Sequential Storage Table that writes data in insertion order
questions.explanation: An SSTable (Sorted String Table) stores key-value pairs sorted by key. Sorting enables binary search for lookups and efficient merge operations during compaction, similar to the merge step in merge sort. This is critical for LSM tree performance.

questions.question: What is the purpose of compaction in LSM trees?
options: To compress data and save disk space
To merge multiple SSTables, removing deleted/overwritten entries and reducing the number of files to search
To defragment the disk for faster sequential reads
To backup data to a remote server
questions.explanation: Compaction merges multiple SSTables into fewer, larger ones. During the merge, it discards tombstones (deleted keys) and keeps only the latest version of each key. Fewer SSTables means reads check fewer files, improving read performance.

questions.question: What is write amplification in the context of database storage engines?
options: When a single write is replicated to multiple database replicas
When a single logical write causes multiple physical writes to disk due to the storage engine's internal structure
When write throughput exceeds read throughput
When a write triggers multiple index updates
questions.explanation: Write amplification means one logical write results in multiple physical disk writes. In B-trees, updating a page may require writing the page plus WAL entry. In LSM trees, data is written to the memtable, then flushed to SSTables, then rewritten during compaction — potentially 10-30x amplification.

questions.question: A B-tree node fits in a 4KB disk page and each key-pointer pair takes 16 bytes. What is the approximate branching factor, and how many keys can a 3-level tree hold?
options: Branching factor ~256, approximately 16 million keys
Branching factor ~64, approximately 262,144 keys
Branching factor ~1024, approximately 1 billion keys
Branching factor ~32, approximately 32,768 keys
questions.explanation: 4KB / 16 bytes = 256 key-pointer pairs per node. A 3-level tree stores up to 256^3 = ~16.7 million keys. This is why B-trees are so efficient for databases — millions of keys with just 3 disk reads per lookup.

questions.question: What is the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and why is it necessary for B-tree databases?
options: A log that records user queries for auditing purposes
An append-only log where every modification is written before updating the B-tree pages, ensuring crash recovery
A cache of recent writes to speed up read queries
A replication log sent to standby servers
questions.explanation: The WAL ensures durability. Before modifying a B-tree page in place, the change is appended to the WAL. If the database crashes mid-write, the WAL can replay uncommitted changes. Without WAL, a crash during a page split could leave the B-tree in a corrupted state.

questions.question: Why do LSM trees suffer from read amplification, and how do Bloom filters help?
options: LSM trees read too much data per query; Bloom filters compress the data
Reads must check the memtable plus multiple SSTables; Bloom filters quickly determine if an SSTable definitely does NOT contain a key, skipping unnecessary reads
LSM trees amplify read requests across replicas; Bloom filters deduplicate the requests
Reads are amplified by the WAL; Bloom filters bypass the WAL
questions.explanation: A read may need to check the memtable and every SSTable level until the key is found. A Bloom filter for each SSTable answers 'definitely not here' with 100% accuracy and 'maybe here' with some false positives. This skips most SSTables, dramatically reducing disk reads.

questions.question: What is the key difference between size-tiered and leveled compaction strategies in LSM trees?
options: Size-tiered is for SSDs and leveled is for HDDs
Size-tiered merges similarly-sized SSTables into larger ones; leveled maintains fixed-size levels where each level is 10x larger, providing better read performance but higher write amplification
Size-tiered uses more memory; leveled uses more disk
There is no practical difference — they are the same algorithm
questions.explanation: Size-tiered compaction merges SSTables of similar size, which is simpler but can leave many overlapping SSTables at a given size tier. Leveled compaction (used by LevelDB/RocksDB) maintains non-overlapping sorted runs at each level, giving better read performance at the cost of more write amplification during compaction.
